questions.title: What is the difference between |-> and |=> in SVA?
questions.answer: Consequent starts in the same cycle (overlapping, `|->`) vs the next cycle (non-overlapping, `|=>`). `a |=> b` is equivalent to `a |-> ##1 b`.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** both are implications that only check the consequent when the antecedent matches. `|->` (overlapping) starts the consequent **in the same cycle** the antecedent ends; `|=>` (non-overlapping) starts it **one cycle later**. `a |=> b` is exactly `a |-> ##1 b`.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",           "wave": "p..." },
  { "name": "a",             "wave": "10.." },
  { "name": "b for a |-> b", "wave": "1x.." },
  { "name": "b for a |=> b", "wave": "x1x." }
],
  "head": { "text": "|-> checks b in the same cycle as a; |=> checks the next cycle", "tick": 1 } }
```

| | `a \|-> b` | `a \|=> b` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name | overlapping | non-overlapping |
| b checked at | cycle of a | cycle after a |
| Equivalent | | `a \|-> ##1 b` |
| Typical use | combinational response, same-cycle rules (`valid \|-> !$isunknown(data)`) | registered response (`wr_en \|=> !empty`, `req \|=> ack`) |

### Explanation
- Both pass **vacuously** when the antecedent is false, so add a `cover property` on the antecedent.
- If the antecedent is a multi-cycle sequence, `|->` starts the consequent on the antecedent's **last** cycle.

```systemverilog
a_same : assert property (@(posedge clk) valid |-> !$isunknown(data));
a_next : assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) wr_en && !full |=> !empty);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using `|->` when the design responds a cycle later (registered output) gives false failures: draw the waveform first.
- `a ##1 b |-> c` checks `c` at b's cycle, not a's.

### Follow-ups
- **Response within 1 to 3 cycles?** `a |-> ##[1:3] b` (or `a |=> ##[0:2] b`).
- **Is `|=>` allowed in a sequence?** No, implication is a property operator; it can't be nested inside a sequence.

questions.title: What is a vacuous pass, and how do you detect it?
questions.answer: Antecedent false: the implication passes without checking anything. Add a `cover property` on the antecedent and check the hit count (and the tool's vacuous-pass statistics).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** for `A |-> C`, every clock where `A` does not match counts as a **vacuous success**: nothing was checked. A property whose antecedent never fires passes the whole simulation and proves nothing. Pair every implication with a `cover` of its antecedent.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",               "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "wr_en (antecedent)", "wave": "0......" },
  { "name": "empty",             "wave": "1......" },
  { "name": "a_wr result",       "wave": "=======", "data": ["vac", "vac", "vac", "vac", "vac", "vac", "vac"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "wr_en |=> !empty: wr_en is never 1, so every attempt passes vacuously" } }
```

| Statistic (VCS/Xcelium report) | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| attempts | clocks where an evaluation started |
| real (non-vacuous) successes | antecedent matched and consequent held |
| vacuous successes | antecedent did not match |
| failures | antecedent matched, consequent failed |

### Explanation
```systemverilog
a_wr : assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) wr_en |=> !empty);
c_wr : cover  property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) wr_en);   // must be > 0
// Stronger: cover the full scenario, not just the trigger
c_wr_full : cover property (@(posedge clk) full ##1 rd_en ##1 wr_en);
```
- A cover hit count of 0 means the check was **never exercised**: a stimulus or coverage hole.
- In formal, an unreachable cover means dead logic or over-constrained assumptions.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A wrong signal name or polarity in the antecedent (`rst_n` vs `rst`) produces silent vacuity.
- `disable iff` held true for the whole sim makes everything "disabled", not checked.

### Follow-ups
- **How do you report vacuity automatically?** Track real-success counts in the coverage report or use the simulator's vacuity reporting; review covers with zero hits.
- **Is a property without implication ever vacuous?** No: `assert property (!(full && empty))` is checked every cycle.

questions.title: Why are concurrent assertions race-free?
questions.answer: Values are sampled in the Preponed region, before any updates in that time step; properties are evaluated in the Observed region and action blocks run in Reactive.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** a concurrent assertion **samples** its signals in the **Preponed** region (before anything changes in that time step) and **evaluates** in the **Observed** region. It sees the same pre-edge values a flip-flop does, so `<=` updates on the same edge can't race it. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Preponed
SAMPLE values for assertions"] --> B["Active
RTL always blocks, blocking assigns"] B --> C["Inactive
#0 events"] C --> D["NBA
nonblocking updates"] D --> E["Observed
EVALUATE properties"] E --> F["Reactive
action blocks, program code"] F --> G["Postponed
$strobe, assert final"] ``` ```wavedrom { "signal": [ { "name": "clk", "wave": "p...." }, { "name": "q (RTL, <=)", "wave": "0.1..", "node": "..a" }, { "name": "q sampled (Preponed)", "wave": "0..1.", "node": "...b" } ], "edge": [ "a~>b seen one edge later" ], "head": { "text": "q updates at edge 2, but assertions at edge 2 still sample 0", "tick": 0 } } ``` ### Explanation - Sampling happens once per time step, before Active, so the order of `always` blocks doesn't matter. - Evaluation in Observed means the property uses only sampled values (except `disable iff`, which uses current values). - Action blocks (`else $error`) run in Reactive, after the design has settled. ### Corner cases & pitfalls - The flip side: an assertion sees a value **one edge later** than the RTL update: `d` driven at edge *n* is visible to the property at edge *n+1*. - Immediate assertions inside `always_comb` are **not** race-free; use deferred (`assert #0` / `assert final`) to filter glitches. - Testbench drives without clocking blocks can still race the *DUT*; the assertion is fine, the stimulus isn't. ### Follow-ups - **Which value does `$rose(x)` compare?** The sampled value at this clock vs the sampled value at the previous clock. - **What uses current (not sampled) values?** `disable iff` and the clocking event itself.

questions.title: What is the difference between [->3] (goto) and [=3] (non-consecutive) repetition?
questions.answer: Goto `[->3]` ends ON the 3rd occurrence; non-consecutive `[=3]` matches the 3rd occurrence and may extend until just before the next occurrence. Interview line: [->n] = "on the nth one"; [=n] = "after the nth one, before the next one".
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** both count non-consecutive occurrences of `b`. **Goto `b[->3]`** ends exactly **on** the 3rd `b`. **Non-consecutive `b[=3]`** matches on the 3rd `b` *and every following cycle until (not including) the next `b`*. The difference only shows when something follows the repetition.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",            "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "b",              "wave": "010101001" },
  {},
  { "name": "b[->3] matches", "wave": "000001000" },
  { "name": "b[=3] matches",  "wave": "000001110" },
  { "name": "b[*3] matches",  "wave": "000000000" }
],
  "head": { "text": "[->3] ends ON the 3rd b; [=3] can stretch until just before the 4th b; [*3] needs 3 consecutive", "tick": 1 } }
```

| Operator | Expansion | Ends |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `b[*3]` | `b ##1 b ##1 b` | after 3 consecutive b |
| `b[->3]` | `(!b[*0:$] ##1 b)[*3]` | on the 3rd b |
| `b[=3]` | `b[->3] ##1 !b[*0:$]` | on the 3rd b or any later cycle before the next b |

### Explanation
With `c` after the repetition (start at cycle 1):
- `b[->3] ##1 c` requires `c` **exactly** the cycle after the 3rd `b` (cycle 7 here).
- `b[=3] ##1 c` accepts `c` at cycle 7, 8 or 9, as long as no 4th `b` came first.

```systemverilog
// exactly the cycle after the 4th beat, the burst must end
a_burst_end : assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(start) |-> beat[->4] ##1 done);
// 3 writes some time before the commit, no extra write before it
a_commit    : assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(open) |-> wr[=3] ##1 commit);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `[->1]` is the common "wait for the next occurrence": `req |-> ack[->1] ##0 data_ok`.
- Unbounded repetitions in an antecedent spawn many threads; wrap with `first_match` or bound them.

### Follow-ups
- **`b[->1:3]`?** Ends on the 1st, 2nd or 3rd occurrence (multiple matches).
- **Equivalent of `b[=3]` with goto?** `b[->3] ##1 !b[*0:$]`.

questions.title: What is the difference between the sequence operators and and intersect?
questions.answer: `and`: both sequences start together; the composite matches when both have matched, ending at the later end. `intersect`: same start and the same end (same length).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** both require two sequences to start at the same cycle and both to match. `s1 and s2` ends when the **later** of the two ends (lengths may differ). `s1 intersect s2` requires them to **end on the same cycle** (same length).

Example, all attempts start at cycle 1: `s1 = a ##[1:3] b` (b true at cycles 2 and 4), `s2 = c ##2 d` (ends at cycle 3).

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p...." },
  { "name": "a",   "wave": "010.." },
  { "name": "b",   "wave": "00101" },
  { "name": "c",   "wave": "010.." },
  { "name": "d",   "wave": "00010" }
],
  "head": { "text": "cycles 1..4: s1 can end at 2 or 4, s2 ends at 3", "tick": 0 } }
```

| Composite | Matches end at | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `s1 or s2` | 2, 3, 4 | any match of either |
| `s1 and s2` | 3, 4 | pairs (2,3) end at 3 and (4,3) end at 4 |
| `s1 intersect s2` | none | s1 ends at 2 or 4, s2 at 3: never the same cycle |

### Explanation
- `intersect` is the tool for **length constraints**: `(req ##[1:$] ack) intersect (1'b1 [*1:8])` means ack arrives within 8 cycles.
- `within` is built from `intersect`: `s1 within s2` = `(1[*0:$] ##1 s1 ##1 1[*0:$]) intersect s2`.
- `throughout` too: `e throughout s` = `(e[*0:$]) intersect s`.

```systemverilog
// handshake must complete in at most 6 cycles
a_len : assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(req) |->
          (req ##[1:$] ack) intersect (1'b1 [*2:6]));
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- With `and`, the composite keeps waiting for the slower sequence: an unbounded `s2` makes the whole thing unbounded.
- `and`/`or` on *properties* are different operators (property conjunction/disjunction) from the *sequence* ones, though they read the same.

### Follow-ups
- **What does `first_match(s1 and s2)` add?** Keeps only the earliest end (cycle 3 here), killing the extra thread.

questions.title: How do you check that output data equals input data from N cycles ago?
questions.answer: `$past(in, N)` for a fixed latency (with an enable/valid qualifier, `$past(x, n, en)` for stalls); use a local variable if the latency is variable.

questions.title: How do you check that a response matches its request ID when the latency is variable?
questions.answer: Use a local variable to capture the ID in the antecedent and compare it in the consequent: `(arvalid && arready, id = arid) |-> ##[1:32] (rvalid && rid == id)`.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** a **local variable** in the property captures the ID when the request handshakes; each attempt is its own thread with its own copy, so many requests can be in flight and each waits for *its* ID.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",     "wave": "p......." },
  { "name": "arvalid", "wave": "010....." },
  { "name": "arid",    "wave": "x=x.....", "data": ["5"], "node": ".a" },
  { "name": "id (local)", "wave": "x=......", "data": ["5"] },
  { "name": "rvalid",  "wave": "0..1.10." },
  { "name": "rid",     "wave": "x..=x=x.", "data": ["3", "5"], "node": ".....b" }
],
  "edge": [ "a~>b match rid == id" ],
  "head": { "text": "capture arid=5; rid=3 is ignored; rid=5 at cycle 5 satisfies the attempt", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
property p_id_resp;
  logic [3:0] id;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (arvalid && arready, id = arid)
      |-> ##[1:32] (rvalid && rready && rlast && rid == id);
endproperty
a_id_resp : assert property (p_id_resp)
  else $error("[%0t] no response for ARID %0d within 32 cycles", $time, $sampled(arid));
c_id_resp : cover  property (p_id_resp);
```

### Explanation
- Syntax: `(expression, var = value)` assigns the local variable when that subsequence matches.
- `##[1:32]` bounds the wait (a safety property, good for simulation and formal). For an unbounded wait use `s_eventually` / `strong(##[1:$] ...)`.
- Local variables can also be used for data integrity: capture the write data with the address and compare on the read.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Two outstanding requests with the **same** ID can both be satisfied by one response: SVA threads don't "consume" matches. Counting outstanding transactions per ID needs an aux model or the scoreboard.
- Only R beats with `rlast` should close a burst; matching any beat passes too early.

### Follow-ups
- **Response must not arrive for an ID that was never requested?** Needs per-ID outstanding counters: aux logic (`cnt[id]`) plus `rvalid |-> cnt[rid] != 0`.

questions.title: Can SVA check in-order completion of many outstanding transactions?
questions.answer: Not cleanly: each attempt is an independent thread. Use an auxiliary counter/queue model (modeling code next to the assertions) or the scoreboard.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** not with pure SVA. Each attempt is an **independent thread**, so assertions can say "every request eventually gets a response" but not "responses come back **in request order**" or "never more than N outstanding". Add a small **auxiliary model** (a tag FIFO / counter in RTL-style code) and assert against it, or leave ordering to the scoreboard. ```mermaid flowchart LR REQ["req_fire, req_id"] --> AUX["aux tag FIFO
wr_ptr / rd_ptr"] RSP["rsp_fire, rsp_id"] --> AUX AUX -->|head_id, count| SVA["a_in_order: rsp_fire implies rsp_id == head_id"] AUX --> SVA2["a_max_out: count never exceeds N"] ``` ### Code (formal-friendly: fixed array, no queues) ```systemverilog module inorder_sva #(parameter int IDW = 4, parameter int DEPTH = 8) ( input logic clk, rst_n, input logic req_fire, rsp_fire, input logic [IDW-1:0] req_id, rsp_id ); localparam int AW = $clog2(DEPTH); logic [IDW-1:0] tag_mem [DEPTH]; logic [AW:0] wr_ptr, rd_ptr; // extra bit tells full from empty wire [AW:0] count = wr_ptr - rd_ptr; always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) if (!rst_n) begin wr_ptr <= '0; rd_ptr <= '0; end else begin if (req_fire) begin tag_mem[wr_ptr[AW-1:0]] <= req_id; wr_ptr <= wr_ptr + 1; end if (rsp_fire) rd_ptr <= rd_ptr + 1; end default clocking @(posedge clk); endclocking default disable iff (!rst_n); a_no_spurious : assert property (rsp_fire |-> count != 0); a_in_order : assert property (rsp_fire |-> rsp_id == tag_mem[rd_ptr[AW-1:0]]); a_max_out : assert property (count <= DEPTH); c_full : cover property (count == DEPTH); endmodule ``` | Check | Pure SVA | Aux model | Scoreboard | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | each req gets a rsp within N | yes | | yes | | response ID matches a request | weak (no consumption) | yes | yes | | in-order completion | no | yes | yes | | data transformation correct | limited | | yes | ### Corner cases & pitfalls - Request and response in the same cycle: the aux model must update both pointers (it does here). - Queues and class objects are not allowed in concurrent assertion expressions; keep aux logic static for formal. ### Follow-ups - **AXI (in order per ID only)?** One tag FIFO per ID, or a per-ID counter plus a scoreboard.

questions.title: What does disable iff do to an in-flight assertion attempt?
questions.answer: Aborts it: the attempt counts as neither pass nor fail. `disable iff` is asynchronous and uses current (not sampled) values. Use `default disable iff (!rst_n);`.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** when the `disable iff` condition becomes true, every attempt in progress is **aborted** and reported as *disabled*: neither a pass nor a failure. The condition is checked **asynchronously** with **current** values, not sampled ones.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "rst_n", "wave": "1..0.1." },
  { "name": "req",   "wave": "010...." },
  { "name": "ack",   "wave": "0......" },
  { "name": "attempt (req |-> ##[1:4] ack)", "wave": "x=.=x..", "data": ["waiting", "DISABLED"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "reset asserts mid-window: the attempt is aborted, not failed", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
module blk_sva (input logic clk, rst_n, req, ack);
  default clocking cb @(posedge clk); endclocking
  default disable iff (!rst_n);       // applies to every assertion below

  a_req_ack : assert property ($rose(req) |-> ##[1:4] ack);

  // $past right after reset can see pre-reset values: guard it
  a_hold : assert property ($past(rst_n) && $past(req && !ack) |-> req);
endmodule
```
- Without it, assertions fire false errors during reset (X on signals, `$past` returning reset/X values).
- Because it is asynchronous, a one-cycle reset glitch between edges still kills in-flight attempts.

| Outcome | Counted as |
| --- | --- |
| antecedent false | vacuous pass |
| consequent holds | real pass |
| consequent fails | failure |
| `disable iff` true during attempt | disabled (neither) |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `disable iff` is only allowed at the top of a property (not nested).
- Too broad a disable condition (e.g. tied to a debug mode always on) silently disables checking: watch the disabled count.
- `accept_on` / `reject_on` are the newer alternatives that turn the abort into a pass or fail.

### Follow-ups
- **Assertion on reset behavior itself?** Write it without `disable iff`: `$rose(rst_n) |-> count == 0`.

questions.title: Why use bind for assertions?
questions.answer: Adds checkers without editing RTL; the designer owns the RTL, the verifier owns the checkers; the same checker binds into every instance and is reused directly in formal (JasperGold).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `bind` instantiates a checker module **inside** a design module (or specific instances) from outside the RTL source. The RTL stays untouched, the checker sees internal signals through port connections, and the same checker runs in simulation and formal.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  RTL["fifo.sv (designer owned)"] --> I1["u_fifo_a"]
  RTL --> I2["u_fifo_b"]
  SVA["fifo_sva.sv (verifier owned)"] --> BIND["bind fifo fifo_sva u_sva (.*)"]
  BIND -->|instantiated inside| I1
  BIND -->|instantiated inside| I2
  BIND --> FV["same bind file in JasperGold"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// every instance of module fifo gets a checker
bind fifo fifo_sva #(.DEPTH(DEPTH)) u_fifo_sva (.*);

// only selected instances
bind fifo: top.u_core.u_fifo_a, top.u_core.u_fifo_b fifo_sva u_fifo_sva (.*);

// explicit connections when names differ
bind fifo fifo_sva u_fifo_sva (.clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .wr_en(push), .rd_en(pop),
                               .full(full), .empty(empty));
```

| Approach | Edits RTL? | Reuse across instances | Sees internals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| assertions inline in RTL | yes | yes | yes |
| assertions in TB via hierarchical paths | no | no (paths per instance) | yes |
| **bind** | no | yes | yes (via ports) |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `.*` needs matching names in the target scope; parameters can reference the target's parameters (`DEPTH`).
- Checker ports should all be **inputs**: a checker must never drive design signals.
- Keep bind files in the verification file list, not compiled into synthesis.

### Follow-ups
- **Bind to an interface?** Yes, `bind` works on modules, interfaces and specific instances.
- **`checker ... endchecker`?** SV's dedicated checker construct, also bindable; plain modules are more common in practice.

questions.title: What do assert, assume and cover mean in formal verification?
questions.answer: Prove / constrain / show reachable. In simulation, assume is checked like assert; cover counts matches.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **assert** = a proof target, **assume** = a constraint on inputs (the legal environment), **cover** = a reachability goal that must produce a trace. In simulation `assume` is just checked like `assert`, and `cover` counts hits.

| Directive | Simulation | Formal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `assert property` | checks, reports failures | must hold on all reachable states; a failure gives a CEX trace |
| `assume property` | checked like an assert (catches a bad stimulus) | restricts input values the tool may choose |
| `cover property` | counts matches (functional coverage) | proves the scenario is reachable and shows a trace |
| `restrict property` | ignored | formal-only state-space pruning |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  ENV["assume: legal inputs"] --> DUT["DUT under proof"]
  DUT --> AS["assert: proven or CEX"]
  DUT --> CV["cover: reachable or unreachable"]
  CV -->|unreachable| WARN["dead logic or over-constrained assumes"]
```

### Explanation
```systemverilog
// Environment rule: the upstream master never drops valid before ready
m_vld_hold : assume property (@(posedge clk) valid && !ready |=> valid);
// DUT promise
a_no_ovf   : assert property (@(posedge clk) full |-> !push_accepted);
// Sanity: can we actually fill the FIFO?
c_full     : cover  property (@(posedge clk) full);
```
- **Assume-guarantee**: the same property is an `assert` on the block that drives a signal and an `assume` on the block that consumes it.
- Always run covers alongside asserts: a proof is only meaningful if the interesting states are reachable.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- **Over-constraining** with assumes makes proofs pass trivially and hides bugs; a conflicting set of assumes can make *everything* pass.
- An assumption on an output of the DUT constrains the design itself: assume inputs only.

### Follow-ups
- **Bounded vs full proof?** Bounded = holds up to N cycles from reset; full = holds for all reachable states.

questions.title: How do you make an eventuality property fail at the end of simulation?
questions.answer: Wrap it in `strong(...)` or use `s_eventually`; `##[1:$]` is weak by default, so an attempt still waiting when the sim ends does not fail.

questions.title: What is the difference between an immediate and a deferred immediate assertion?
questions.answer: Deferred (`assert #0` / `assert final`) reports after zero-delay glitches settle in the time step; simple immediate reports as soon as the statement executes. `assert final` reports in the Postponed region.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** a **simple immediate** assertion checks the expression the instant the statement executes, so in `always_comb` it can fire on a **zero-delay glitch** while signals are still settling. A **deferred** assertion (`assert #0` or `assert final`) queues its report and only reports the result of the **last** evaluation in that time step.

| Event within one time step | `sel` | simple `assert` | `assert #0` | `assert final` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| comb logic evaluates first input | 3 (glitch) | **fails** | pending (flushed) | pending (flushed) |
| second input settles | 1 | passes | pending | pending |
| Observed / Reactive | 1 | | reports pass | |
| Postponed | 1 | | | reports pass |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p..." },
  { "name": "sel (with 0-delay glitch)", "wave": "=.=.", "data": ["0", "3 then 1"] },
  { "name": "simple assert", "wave": "x.=x", "data": ["false error"] },
  { "name": "assert #0 / final", "wave": "x.=x", "data": ["pass"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "the glitch to 3 exists only inside one time step" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
always_comb assert (!(rd_en && empty)) else $error("read on empty");   // simple: glitch-prone
always_comb assert #0   (sel inside {[0:2]});      // observed deferred
always_comb assert final ($onehot0(grant));         // final deferred, Postponed region
```

### Explanation
- `#0` deferred: report scheduled in the Reactive region; `final`: in Postponed, after everything (including program code) settled.
- Deferred assertions are allowed outside procedural code too (`assert #0 (...)` at module level acts like an `always_comb`).
- Action blocks of deferred assertions may contain only a single subroutine call.

### Follow-ups
- **Immediate vs concurrent?** Immediate: no clock, current values, one point in time. Concurrent: clocked, sampled values, temporal.

questions.title: Write assertions: valid must stay high and data must stay stable until ready (valid/ready handshake)
questions.prompt: For a valid/ready (AXI-style) channel: once `valid` is asserted it must not drop until `ready` is seen, and `data` must hold while stalled. Write the must-have protocol assertions plus covers, as a bindable checker.
questions.answer: `valid && !ready |=> valid`, `valid && !ready |=> $stable(data)`, plus `valid |-> !$isunknown(data)` and a cover for a stall.

questions.title: Write an assertion: a Gray-coded pointer changes at most one bit per clock
questions.prompt: An async FIFO passes its write pointer to the read domain in Gray code. Write an assertion that the Gray pointer changes at most one bit per clock (in its own clock domain).
questions.answer: `$past(rst_n) |-> $countones(gray_ptr ^ $past(gray_ptr)) <= 1` (equivalently `$onehot0(gray_ptr ^ $past(gray_ptr))`), clocked in the pointer's own domain.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** XOR the current and previous pointer values: the result has a 1 for each bit that changed. A Gray pointer must change **0 or 1** bits per clock, so `$countones(...) <= 1` (or `$onehot0(...)`). Clock it on the **source** domain and skip the first cycle out of reset.

| wr_bin | gray = bin ^ (bin >> 1) | gray ^ $past(gray) | ones |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 000 | | |
| 1 | 001 | 001 | 1 |
| 2 | 011 | 010 | 1 |
| 3 | 010 | 001 | 1 |
| 4 | 110 | 100 | 1 |
| 7 -> 0 (wrap) | 100 -> 000 | 100 | 1 |
| bug: binary 3 -> 4 sent | 011 -> 100 | 111 | **3: fail** |

### Code
```systemverilog
module gray_sva #(parameter int W = 4) (
  input logic         wclk, wrst_n,
  input logic [W-1:0] wptr_gray
);
  a_gray_1bit : assert property (@(posedge wclk) disable iff (!wrst_n)
                  $past(wrst_n) |-> $countones(wptr_gray ^ $past(wptr_gray)) <= 1)
    else $error("[%0t] gray pointer changed %0d bits", $time,
                $countones(wptr_gray ^ $past(wptr_gray)));

  // equivalent form
  a_gray_oh0  : assert property (@(posedge wclk) disable iff (!wrst_n)
                  $past(wrst_n) |-> $onehot0(wptr_gray ^ $past(wptr_gray)));

  // the pointer actually moves (non-vacuous)
  c_gray_move : cover property (@(posedge wclk) wptr_gray != $past(wptr_gray));
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- Why it matters: the read domain samples the pointer through a 2-flop synchronizer. If only one bit changes, a metastable sample resolves to either the old or the new value; both are safe. Multi-bit changes can produce a torn value that was never a real pointer.
- `$past(wrst_n)` guard avoids comparing against the reset value on the first cycle.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Clock it on the **write** clock: sampling on the read clock can legitimately see multiple increments between samples.
- The *synchronized* copy in the read domain may change by more than one bit between read clocks if wclk is faster; check the source register, not the sync output.
- The pointer must also be **registered** (no glitchy combinational Gray logic crossing the domain): a structural CDC check, not an assertion.

### Follow-ups
- **Non-power-of-two depth?** Plain Gray wrap breaks the one-bit rule; this assertion catches it.

questions.title: Write assertions: a FIFO never overflows or underflows (as a bound checker)
questions.prompt: A synchronous FIFO module `fifo` has ports `clk, rst_n, wr_en, rd_en, full, empty` and parameter `DEPTH`. Write a checker that the FIFO never overflows or underflows and that its flags are consistent, and attach it without editing the RTL.
questions.answer: Checker module with `default clocking` and `default disable iff`: `full |-> !wr_en`, `empty |-> !rd_en`, `!(full && empty)`, `cover ($rose(full))`; attach with `bind fifo fifo_sva #(.DEPTH(DEPTH)) u_fifo_sva (.*);`.

questions.title: Assertions vs scoreboard: when do you use which?
questions.answer: SVA for local, cycle-accurate protocol rules (catches the bug at the cycle and location). Scoreboard for end-to-end data correctness, ordering and transformations.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **assertions** check *local, cycle-accurate rules* right where and when they are broken; a **scoreboard** checks *end-to-end data correctness* (ordering, transformations, missing/extra transactions) at the transaction level. Real environments use both.

| | SVA | Scoreboard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Level | signals, cycles | transactions |
| Best for | handshakes, stability, one-hot, timeouts, Gray, FIFO flags | data integrity, ordering, reference model compare |
| Catches the bug | at the exact cycle and signal | later, at the comparison point |
| Location | bound to the RTL block (reused in formal) | UVM env |
| Reuse | block, subsystem, formal | block to SoC with the agent |
| Weak at | many outstanding transactions, complex math | cycle-level timing rules |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  DUT["DUT"] -->|pins| SVA["bound SVA: protocol rules at each cycle"]
  DUT -->|pins| MON["monitor"]
  MON -->|transactions| SCB["scoreboard: expected vs actual"]
  REF["reference model"] --> SCB
```

### Explanation
- Example: an AXI crossbar sends W data to two slaves at once. A one-hot assertion on `s_wvalid` fires at **that cycle**; a scoreboard would only notice a wrong memory value at the end of the test.
- Conversely "read returns the last written data after reordering" is natural in a scoreboard and painful in SVA.

### Follow-ups
- **Overlap?** Fine: an assertion can catch the root cause earlier while the scoreboard confirms end-to-end correctness.
- **Where do you check reset values?** Assertions (`$rose(rst_n) |-> ...`) or a reset sequence in RAL.

questions.title: How do assertions contribute to coverage?
questions.answer: `cover property` hits are functional coverage. Assertion pass/fail/vacuous counts appear in the coverage report (VCS/Verdi) and map to verification plan items.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `cover property` / `cover sequence` statements are **functional coverage points** that count temporal scenarios, and every assertion's attempt/pass/fail/vacuous statistics land in the coverage database. Both can be linked to verification-plan items.

| Construct | Counts | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cover property (p)` | each successful match of p | temporal scenarios: stall then transfer, back-to-back |
| `cover sequence (s)` | every match, including multiple per attempt | counting occurrences |
| assertion statistics | attempts, real passes, vacuous passes, failures | proving checks were exercised |
| covergroup | value bins / crosses | data-value coverage |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  COV["cover property hits"] --> DB["coverage DB (vdb / ucdb)"]
  ASTAT["assert pass / fail / vacuous counts"] --> DB
  CG["covergroups"] --> DB
  DB --> VP["vplan items in Verdi / vManager"]
```

### Code
```systemverilog
// Temporal scenarios that a covergroup can't express easily
c_stall_xfer : cover property (@(posedge clk) valid && !ready [*2:$] ##1 valid && ready);
c_full_empty : cover property (@(posedge clk) full ##[1:$] empty);
// Antecedent cover keeps an implication honest
c_req        : cover property (@(posedge clk) $rose(req));
```

### Explanation
- Assertion coverage tells you a check was **non-vacuously exercised**; it is not the same as "the feature works".
- In formal, a cover returning *unreachable* is a strong signal of dead logic or over-constraint.

### Follow-ups
- **Cover property vs covergroup?** Cover property for sequences over time; covergroups for values and crosses (can be sampled from a sequence match via a function call in the match item).

questions.title: Compare immediate and concurrent assertions
questions.answer: Immediate: procedural, evaluated when the statement executes, current values, `assert (expr)`. Concurrent: clocked, temporal, sampled (Preponed) values, `assert property`, in module/interface/program/bind.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** an **immediate** assertion is a procedural `if` with reporting: no clock, checked when the statement runs, using current values. A **concurrent** assertion is clocked and temporal: it samples values at the clock edge and can span many cycles.

| | Immediate | Concurrent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | procedural code (`always`, `initial`, tasks, class methods) | module, interface, program, checker, `bind`; also in `always` (inferred clock) |
| Timing | when the statement executes | every clock edge, across cycles |
| Values | current (glitch-prone) | sampled in Preponed |
| Keyword | `assert (expr)` | `assert property (...)` |
| Temporal operators | no | `##`, `[*]`, `\|->`, `$past`... |
| Use | single-point checks in a checker/scoreboard/model | protocol rules over time |

```systemverilog
// Immediate (simple) and deferred
always_comb assert (!(rd_en && empty)) else $error("read on empty");
always_comb assert final ($onehot0(grant));

// In a UVM scoreboard (classes can only use immediate assertions)
assert (tr.addr inside {[0:'hFFF]}) else `uvm_error("SB", "addr out of range")

// Concurrent
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) req |-> ##[1:4] ack);
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Q{"Does the rule involve time or a clock?"} -->|no| IMM["immediate assert (deferred if in always_comb)"]
  Q -->|yes| CONC["concurrent assert property"]
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Concurrent assertions are **not allowed in classes**; use immediate ones or put SVA in an interface.
- Simple immediate assertions in `always_comb` can fire on delta glitches: use `assert #0` / `assert final`.

### Follow-ups
- **Concurrent assertion inside an `always @(posedge clk)` block?** Allowed; the clock is inferred from the block and the enclosing `if` becomes part of the antecedent.

questions.title: Explain the anatomy of an SVA check: sequence, property and directive
questions.answer: sequence = a pattern over time; property = clock + reset + implication around sequences; directive = assert / assume / cover (restrict for formal). Name every directive and give it an action block.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** three layers. A **sequence** describes a pattern over cycles, a **property** adds the clock, reset and implication (the rule), and a **directive** (`assert`, `assume`, `cover`, `restrict`) says what the tool should do with it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SEQ["sequence s_req_ack: req ##[1:3] ack"] --> PROP["property p_handshake: clock + disable iff + implication"]
  PROP --> A["assert: check, report failure"]
  PROP --> M["assume: constrain inputs"]
  PROP --> C["cover: did it happen?"]
```

### Code
```systemverilog
sequence s_req_ack;
  req ##[1:3] ack;                       // a pattern over time
endsequence

property p_handshake;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    $rose(req) |-> s_req_ack;            // implication + clock + reset
endproperty

a_handshake : assert property (p_handshake)
  else `uvm_error("SVA", "ack not seen within 3 cycles of req")
c_handshake : cover  property (p_handshake);

// Parameterized and reusable
property p_resp_within(logic trig, logic resp, int unsigned max);
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) trig |-> ##[1:max] resp;
endproperty
a_rd : assert property (p_resp_within(rd_req, rd_ack, 8));
```

| Layer | Contains | Can be reused |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sequence | `##`, repetition, `and/or/intersect`, local vars | in other sequences and properties |
| property | clock, `disable iff`, `\|->`/`\|=>`, `not`, `strong` | by several directives |
| directive | `assert` / `assume` / `cover` / `restrict` + label + action block | n/a |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Label every directive (`a_handshake:`); unlabeled assertions get tool-generated names that are hard to waive or control.
- A `sequence` with a clock can be used standalone with `cover sequence`, and its `.triggered` can be used elsewhere.

### Follow-ups
- **Live-coding process?** 1) draw the waveform, 2) pick `|->` or `|=>`, 3) write the assertion with `default clocking` / `default disable iff`, 4) add a cover for the antecedent.

questions.title: Explain SVA delay and consecutive repetition operators (##n, ##[m:n], [*n], ##[1:$])
questions.answer: `a ##2 b` b exactly 2 cycles after a; `a ##[1:3] b` 1 to 3 cycles; `a ##[1:$] b` eventually (weak by default); `a[*3]` = a a a consecutive; `a[*2:4]` 2 to 4 consecutive cycles.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `##` moves forward in clock cycles; `[*n]` repeats a sequence on **consecutive** cycles. Ranges (`##[1:3]`, `[*2:4]`) create several possible matches (one thread each), and `$` means unbounded.

| Operator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `a ##2 b` | b exactly 2 cycles after a |
| `a ##[1:3] b` | b 1 to 3 cycles after a |
| `a ##[1:$] b` | b eventually (weak by default) |
| `a ##0 b` | b in the same cycle a ends (fusion) |
| `a[*3]` | a a a, consecutive |
| `a[*2:4]` | a for 2 to 4 consecutive cycles |
| `a[*0:$]` | zero or more cycles of a |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "a",   "wave": "01..0.." },
  { "name": "b",   "wave": "0....10" },
  {},
  { "name": "a[*3] matches", "wave": "0..10.." },
  { "name": "a[*3] ##2 b",   "wave": "0....10" }
],
  "head": { "text": "a is high 3 consecutive cycles (1-3), b two cycles after the last a", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
// busy must stay high 2 to 4 cycles after start, then done
a_busy : assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(start) |-> busy[*2:4] ##1 done);
// grant 1 to 3 cycles after request
a_gnt  : assert property (@(posedge clk) req |-> ##[1:3] gnt);
// a pulse is exactly one cycle wide
a_pulse: assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(p) |=> !p);
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `##[1:$]` in an **antecedent** spawns a new thread every cycle: slow sims; use `first_match` or a bound.
- `##[1:$]` in a consequent is **weak**: a hang doesn't fail (use `strong` or a bound).
- `a[*0]` is an empty match; `a[*0] ##1 b` behaves like `b`, which surprises people.

### Follow-ups
- **Non-consecutive repetition?** `[->n]` (goto) and `[=n]`.

questions.title: Explain the SVA sampled-value functions: $rose, $fell, $stable, $changed, $past
questions.answer: $rose LSB 0->1, $fell LSB 1->0, $stable unchanged, $changed = !$stable, $past(x,n) value n clocks ago, $past(x,n,en) counting only enabled clocks. Others: $onehot, $onehot0, $isunknown, $countones. Pitfall: $rose checks only the LSB of a vector.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** these functions compare **sampled** values at the current clock with those at the previous clock. They make edge and stability rules one-liners, but `$rose/$fell` look only at the **LSB** of a vector.

| Function | True when (sampled values) |
| --- | --- |
| `$rose(x)` | LSB of x went 0 -> 1 since the last clock |
| `$fell(x)` | LSB of x went 1 -> 0 |
| `$stable(x)` | x unchanged since the last clock |
| `$changed(x)` | `!$stable(x)` |
| `$past(x, n)` | x from n clocks ago (default 1) |
| `$past(x, n, en)` | x from n clocks *where `en` was true* |
| `$onehot(x)` / `$onehot0(x)` | exactly one / at most one bit set |
| `$isunknown(x)` | any bit X or Z |
| `$countones(x)` | number of 1 bits |

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",        "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "x",          "wave": "0.1..0." },
  { "name": "$rose(x)",   "wave": "0.10..." },
  { "name": "$fell(x)",   "wave": "0....10" },
  { "name": "$stable(x)", "wave": "1.01.01" }
],
  "head": { "text": "evaluated at each edge from the sampled values", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
// Pipeline with 2-cycle latency
a_pipe : assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
           out_valid |-> out_data == $past(in_data, 2) + 1);

// Bus pitfall: $rose(state) only sees state[0]
a_bad  : assert property (@(posedge clk) $rose(state) |-> ...);          // wrong for a bus
a_good : assert property (@(posedge clk) (state == BUSY && $past(state) != BUSY) |-> ...);
// Or: $changed(addr) for any change on a bus
a_addr : assert property (@(posedge clk) valid && !ready |=> !$changed(addr));
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `$rose(x)` is also true when x goes X -> 1 on the first sampled clock; combine with reset guards.
- `$past` in the first cycles after reset returns pre-reset values: guard with `$past(rst_n)`.
- `$stable` treats X -> X as stable; add `!$isunknown` where it matters.

### Follow-ups
- **Use these outside assertions?** Yes, with a clocking event argument: `$rose(x, @(posedge clk))` in procedural code.

questions.title: Explain throughout, within, first_match and .triggered in SVA
questions.answer: `e throughout s`: e holds every cycle of s. `s1 within s2`: s1 occurs entirely inside s2's span. `first_match(s)`: only the earliest match (kills extra threads). `s.triggered`: s has ended in the current cycle (use in another property).

questions.title: Write request/acknowledge assertions with a timeout
questions.prompt: A requester raises `req` and must hold it until `ack`. The responder must answer within 8 cycles. Write the assertions (with covers).
questions.answer: `$rose(req) |-> ##[1:8] ack` (ack within 8 cycles) and `req && !ack |=> req` (req held until ack).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** two rules, one per side. **Responder**: `ack` within 1..8 cycles of a new request (bounded, so a hang fails at cycle 8). **Requester**: `req` must not drop before `ack`.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p.........." },
  { "name": "req", "wave": "01...0....." },
  { "name": "ack", "wave": "0...10....." },
  { "name": "window", "wave": "0.=.......0", "data": ["ack allowed in cycles 2..9"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "$rose(req) at cycle 1; ack at cycle 4 satisfies ##[1:8]; req held until ack", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module req_ack_sva (input logic clk, rst_n, req, ack);
  default clocking cb @(posedge clk); endclocking
  default disable iff (!rst_n);

  a_req_ack  : assert property ($rose(req) |-> ##[1:8] ack)
    else $error("[%0t] ack timeout (> 8 cycles)", $time);
  a_req_hold : assert property (req && !ack |=> req)
    else $error("[%0t] req dropped before ack", $time);
  a_no_spur  : assert property (ack |-> req);          // no ack without a request

  c_fast : cover property ($rose(req) ##1 ack);
  c_slow : cover property ($rose(req) ##8 ack);        // hit the boundary
endmodule
```

| Assertion | Owner side | Fails when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a_req_ack` | responder | ack later than 8 cycles (or never) |
| `a_req_hold` | requester | req withdrawn early |
| `a_no_spur` | responder | ack with no request |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Using `req` instead of `$rose(req)` in the antecedent starts a new attempt every cycle req is high; each attempt has its own 8-cycle window, which may hide a slow response.
- If `ack` can come in the same cycle, use `##[0:8]`.
- Four-phase protocol: also check `!req && ack |=> !req` (don't re-request until ack drops).

### Follow-ups
- **Unbounded but must eventually happen?** `$rose(req) |-> s_eventually ack`.

questions.title: Write arbiter assertions: one-hot grant, grant only to requesters, and no starvation
questions.prompt: An N-requester arbiter has `req[N-1:0]` and `gnt[N-1:0]`. Write assertions that: at most one grant is active, a grant only goes to an active requester, and no requester waits more than 16 cycles.
questions.answer: `$onehot0(gnt)`; `|gnt |-> |(gnt & req)` (only grant a requester); `req[0] |-> ##[1:16] gnt[0]` (fairness bound).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** three classic arbiter properties: **mutual exclusion** (`$onehot0`), **validity** (grant implies request), and **fairness** (bounded wait). Generate the fairness check per requester.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",    "wave": "p......" },
  { "name": "req[0]", "wave": "01....0" },
  { "name": "req[1]", "wave": "01..0.." },
  { "name": "gnt[0]", "wave": "0...1.0" },
  { "name": "gnt[1]", "wave": "0.1.0.." }
],
  "head": { "text": "grants never overlap; req[0] waits 3 cycles (within the 16-cycle bound)", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module arb_sva #(parameter int N = 4) (
  input logic         clk, rst_n,
  input logic [N-1:0] req, gnt
);
  default clocking cb @(posedge clk); endclocking
  default disable iff (!rst_n);

  a_onehot  : assert property ($onehot0(gnt));
  a_gnt_req : assert property (|gnt |-> |(gnt & req));      // only grant a requester
  a_no_x    : assert property (!$isunknown(gnt));

  for (genvar i = 0; i < N; i++) begin : g_fair
    a_no_starv : assert property (req[i] && !gnt[i] |-> ##[1:16] gnt[i])
      else $error("[%0t] requester %0d starved", $time, i);
    c_gnt      : cover  property (req[i] ##[1:$] gnt[i]);
  end

  c_contend : cover property ($countones(req) == N);        // all request at once
endmodule
```

| Property | Type | Catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a_onehot` | safety | two masters granted, bus contention |
| `a_gnt_req` | safety | grant to an idle requester |
| `a_no_starv` | bounded liveness | broken round-robin pointer |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If `gnt` is registered (one cycle after `req`), `a_gnt_req` must compare against the previous request: `|gnt |-> |(gnt & $past(req))`.
- Fairness assumes requesters hold `req` until granted; add that as an assume in formal, or the bound can't be proven.
- The bound (16) must match the arbitration scheme: round-robin with N requesters and max hold time H gives roughly N x H.

### Follow-ups
- **Locked/burst grants?** Add `gnt[i] && lock |=> gnt[i]` (grant held while locked).

questions.title: Write CDC handshake and pulse-synchronizer assertions (source-domain side)
questions.prompt:
1. A 4-phase req/ack handshake carries `data` from `src_clk` to `dst_clk`. Write the source-domain assertions (`ack_sync` is the synchronized ack).
2. A toggle/pulse synchronizer moves single-cycle pulses from a fast clock to a slow clock. Write an assertion that input pulses are spaced far enough apart.
questions.answer: 4-phase handshake: `req && !ack_sync |=> $stable(data)` and `req && !ack_sync |=> req` on src_clk. Pulse sync: `$rose(pulse) |=> !pulse [*4]` on fast_clk so the slow domain sees each pulse.

questions.title: Write AXI crossbar routing assertions (write data to one slave, read data back to the right master)
questions.prompt: An AXI crossbar connects M masters to S slaves. Write assertions that (1) a write data beat is routed to exactly one slave, and (2) a read response is returned to the master that issued the read (use the AR ID).
questions.answer: `|s_wvalid |-> $onehot(s_wvalid)` (W data goes to exactly one slave per beat). Read response must return to the master that issued the ID: track with a local variable. Talking point: both crossbar routing bugs (W to several slaves, R to the wrong master under contention) are caught at the cycle they happen.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** routing bugs are **cycle-local**, so assertions catch them at the exact beat. Rule 1 is a one-hot check on the slave-side `wvalid` vector. Rule 2 needs a **local variable**: capture the ID when master *m*'s AR handshakes, then require an R beat with that ID **at master m**, and none of that tag elsewhere.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M0["master 0"] --> XBAR["crossbar"]
  M1["master 1"] --> XBAR
  XBAR -->|s_wvalid one-hot| S0["slave 0"]
  XBAR --> S1["slave 1"]
  S1 -->|R beat tagged with master id| XBAR
  XBAR -->|R to master m only| M1
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module xbar_sva #(parameter int M = 2, S = 2, IDW = 4) (
  input logic           clk, rst_n,
  input logic [S-1:0]   s_wvalid,
  input logic [M-1:0]   m_arvalid, m_arready, m_rvalid, m_rready, m_rlast,
  input logic [IDW-1:0] m_arid [M],
  input logic [IDW-1:0] m_rid  [M]
);
  default clocking cb @(posedge clk); endclocking
  default disable iff (!rst_n);

  // 1. W beat goes to exactly one slave
  a_w_one_slave : assert property (|s_wvalid |-> $onehot(s_wvalid))
    else $error("[%0t] W data broadcast to slaves %b", $time, s_wvalid);

  // 2. R response returns to the issuing master
  for (genvar m = 0; m < M; m++) begin : g_m
    property p_r_return;
      logic [IDW-1:0] id;
      (m_arvalid[m] && m_arready[m], id = m_arid[m])
        |-> ##[1:64] (m_rvalid[m] && m_rready[m] && m_rlast[m] && m_rid[m] == id);
    endproperty
    a_r_return : assert property (p_r_return)
      else $error("[%0t] master %0d: read response missing or misrouted", $time, m);
    c_r_return : cover  property (p_r_return);
  end

  // Contention cover: both masters reading at once
  c_rd_contend : cover property (&m_arvalid);
endmodule
```

| Bug | Assertion that fires | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| W beat reaches two slaves | `a_w_one_slave` | the same cycle |
| R returned to the wrong master under contention | `a_r_return` (that master times out) | at the 64-cycle bound |
| scoreboard only | data mismatch | end of transaction or test |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The local-variable property doesn't consume matches: two outstanding reads with the same ID can be satisfied by one response; per-ID counting belongs in an aux model or scoreboard.
- Add a negative check with an aux table of outstanding IDs per master: `m_rvalid[m] |-> outstanding[m][m_rid[m]] != 0` catches a response delivered to a master that never asked.
- AXI allows reordering across IDs, so only check order **within** an ID.

### Follow-ups
- **Story:** "I found two routing bugs (W to several slaves, R to the wrong master under contention); a one-hot and an ID-match assertion pinpoint the exact cycle instead of an end-of-test scoreboard mismatch."

questions.title: Strong vs weak properties: what is liveness and how is it handled in simulation vs formal?
questions.answer: In a property `##[1:$] b` is weak: if the sim ends before b it does not fail. `strong(...)` / `s_eventually` make an unfinished attempt fail. In formal, liveness needs fairness assumptions; bounded safety (`##[1:N]`) is usually preferred.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** a **safety** property says "nothing bad ever happens" (a finite trace can show a failure). A **liveness** property says "something good eventually happens" (only an infinite trace can show a failure). SVA operators come in **weak** (an unfinished obligation is OK when the trace ends) and **strong** (it must be fulfilled) flavors.

| Weak (default) | Strong | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `##[1:$] b` in a property | `strong(##[1:$] b)` | b eventually |
| `eventually [m:n] p` | `s_eventually p` | p at some future cycle |
| `nexttime p` | `s_nexttime p` | p next cycle (and the next cycle must exist) |
| `p until q` | `p s_until q` | q must eventually occur |
| `always p` | `s_always [m:n] p` | |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  P["req implies ack eventually"] --> S1{"simulation"}
  P --> F1{"formal"}
  S1 -->|weak| W["pending at end of sim: no failure"]
  S1 -->|strong| ST["pending at end of sim: failure"]
  F1 -->|liveness| L["needs fairness assumptions, CEX is a lasso loop"]
  F1 -->|bounded window| B["safety proof, simple CEX"]
```

### Code
```systemverilog
a_live    : assert property (@(posedge clk) req |-> s_eventually ack);
a_live2   : assert property (@(posedge clk) req |-> strong(##[1:$] ack));
a_bounded : assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) req |-> ##[1:32] ack);

// Formal fairness: the environment eventually lets the arbiter grant
m_fair    : assume property (@(posedge clk) s_eventually !busy);
```

### Explanation
- In formal, a liveness counterexample is a **lasso**: a reachable loop where `ack` never comes. Proving liveness typically requires fairness assumes (e.g., the downstream eventually becomes ready).
- Bounded versions turn liveness into safety: easier to prove and the bound documents the latency spec. Use liveness when no bound exists (e.g., deadlock-freedom).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Strong properties in simulation fail at `$finish` for legitimately in-flight transactions: drain traffic before ending.
- Over-strong fairness assumes can hide real deadlocks.

### Follow-ups
- **Deadlock check?** Liveness: "if valid, eventually ready" with fairness on the consumer, or a bounded "no state stuck for N cycles".

questions.title: What are the expect statement and assertion control tasks ($assertoff, $asserton, $assertkill)?
questions.answer: `expect (@(posedge clk) ##[1:10] done) else ...` is a blocking property check in procedural / sequence code. `$assertoff(0, top.dut.u_sva)` / `$asserton` turn assertions off/on (e.g. during error-injection tests); `$assertkill` also kills in-flight attempts.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `expect` is a **blocking, procedural** property check: the calling thread waits until the property passes or fails, which makes it handy in tests and sequences. The assertion **control** system tasks turn assertions off/on at runtime, e.g. around error injection or reset sequences.

```wavedrom
{ "signal": [
  { "name": "clk",   "wave": "p.........." },
  { "name": "start", "wave": "010........" },
  { "name": "done",  "wave": "0.....10..." },
  { "name": "thread", "wave": "x=....=x...", "data": ["blocked in expect", "continues"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "expect (@(posedge clk) ##[1:10] done) blocks the thread until done or failure", "tick": 0 } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
initial begin
  @(posedge clk) start = 1;
  @(posedge clk) start = 0;
  expect (@(posedge clk) ##[1:10] done)
    else `uvm_error("EXP", "done timeout")
  // runs only after expect resolves
end

// Error-injection test: silence the protocol checker, then restore it
initial begin
  $assertoff(0, top.dut.u_sva);   // 0 = all levels below this scope
  inject_parity_error();
  $assertkill(0, top.dut.u_sva);  // also kill attempts already in flight
  $asserton(0, top.dut.u_sva);
end
```

| Task | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `$assertoff(levels, scope)` | stop **new** attempts; in-flight ones finish |
| `$assertkill(levels, scope)` | stop new attempts **and** abort in-flight ones |
| `$asserton(levels, scope)` | re-enable |
| `$assertcontrol(type, ...)` | 1800-2012 general form (also controls pass/fail/vacuous action blocks) |
| `$assertpassoff` / `$assertfailoff` | silence action blocks only |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `expect` with an unbounded range can hang the thread: bound it or wrap with a timeout `fork`.
- Turning assertions off globally (`$assertoff;`) hides real bugs: scope it to the checker and re-enable it.
- In UVM, a cleaner alternative is demoting specific messages via report catchers, but `$assertoff` is the standard for SVA.

### Follow-ups
- **`expect` vs `wait`?** `wait` blocks on a level; `expect` evaluates a full temporal property and has pass/fail actions.

questions.title: Explain the formal verification (JasperGold) concepts: CEX, bounded vs full proof, assume-guarantee, over-constraint
questions.answer: assume constrains inputs (over-constraining hides bugs); cover proves reachability (unreachable = dead logic or over-constraint); CEX = counterexample trace; bounded proof = up to N cycles; full proof = all reachable states; assume-guarantee = assertions on block A become assumptions on block B. Be ready to explain what was proven and under which assumptions.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** formal tools explore *all* input sequences allowed by the assumptions. An assertion is either **proven** (fully or up to a bound), **failed** with a **counterexample (CEX)** trace, or undetermined. Credibility comes from the **assumptions** and **covers**, so be ready to say what was proven and under which constraints.

| Concept | One-liner |
| --- | --- |
| `assume` | constrains the inputs; over-constraining hides bugs |
| `cover` | proves a state is reachable; unreachable = dead logic or over-constraint |
| CEX | shortest trace from reset that violates the assertion |
| Bounded proof | holds for all traces up to N cycles from reset |
| Full proof | holds for all reachable states (induction / abstraction) |
| Assume-guarantee | assertions on block A become assumptions on block B |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["block A: assert out_valid_hold"] -->|proven then reused as| B["block B: assume in_valid_hold"]
  B --> BP["prove block B assertions"]
  BP --> COV["run covers: are key states reachable?"]
  COV -->|unreachable| FIX["relax assumptions or find dead logic"]
```

### Explanation
- **Bounded vs full:** a bounded proof at depth 40 is meaningful only if the design's interesting behavior (e.g., FIFO full) is reachable within 40 cycles; check with covers.
- **Assume-guarantee** splits a big proof into blocks: each block's outputs are proven, then reused as constraints on the neighbor's inputs.
- **CDC story:** structural CDC checks (sync on every crossing, no reconvergence) plus protocol assertions (handshake order, data stable, Gray one-bit change) proven in JasperGold: "0 violations, under assumptions X and Y, with covers for full/empty reached".

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Conflicting assumes make the tool find **no** legal trace, so every assertion "passes".
- Assuming DUT outputs constrains the design under test itself.
- Large counters/memories cause state explosion: use abstractions, smaller parameters, or cut points.

### Follow-ups
- **How do you debug a CEX?** Check whether it is a real bug or a missing assumption (illegal input); if illegal, add the assume and re-run, then confirm with covers.

questions.title: What are the common SVA pitfalls, and how do you write an assertion during a live-coding interview?
questions.answer: Vacuous pass (no cover), missing disable iff, $rose on a bus, unbounded ##[1:$] in antecedent, weak eventuality, clock mismatch, over-constrained assume, == with X, overlapping implication by mistake. Template: default clocking + default disable iff, draw waveform, pick |-> or |=>, add a cover; bind it.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** most SVA bugs are about **when** something is checked (wrong implication, wrong clock, reset) or **whether** it is checked at all (vacuity, weak properties). A fixed live-coding routine avoids them: draw the waveform, choose the implication, add reset and a cover.

| Pitfall | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| vacuous pass | assertion never fails, never exercised | `cover property` on the antecedent |
| missing `disable iff` | false failures during reset | `default disable iff (!rst_n)` |
| `$rose` on a bus | only LSB checked | compare explicitly or `$changed` |
| `##[1:$]` in antecedent | thread explosion, slow sim | `first_match` or a bound |
| weak eventuality | a hang never fails | `strong` / `s_eventually` / `##[1:N]` |
| wrong clock | misses or false fails in multi-clock designs | `@(posedge src_clk)` explicitly |
| over-constrained `assume` | proofs pass trivially | run covers |
| `==` with X | unknown result | add `!$isunknown(...)` |
| `\|->` instead of `\|=>` | off-by-one-cycle failures | draw the waveform first |

### Live-coding template
```systemverilog
module blk_sva (input logic clk, rst_n /*, ports */);
  default clocking cb @(posedge clk); endclocking
  default disable iff (!rst_n);

  // 1. Draw the waveform. 2. Pick |-> or |=>. 3. Add a cover for the antecedent.
  a_rule : assert property (antecedent |=> consequent)
    else $error("[%0t] rule violated", $time);
  c_rule : cover  property (antecedent);
endmodule

bind blk blk_sva u_sva (.*);
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  W["draw waveform"] --> I["choose |-> or |=>"]
  I --> R["clock + disable iff"]
  R --> A["write assert with message"]
  A --> C["add cover for antecedent"]
  C --> B["bind to the RTL"]
```

### Follow-ups
- **How do you validate an assertion itself?** Inject a bug (or force the signal) and watch it fail; check the cover counts are non-zero.
